summary: Fulvestrant is a selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) and pure estrogen receptor antagonist used in postmenopausal women with hormone receptor (HR)-positive advanced or metastatic breast cancer. It is given alone as first-line therapy in women not previously treated with endocrine therapy or after progression on endocrine therapy, and in combination with the CDK4/6 inhibitors palbociclib, abemaciclib, or ribociclib for HR-positive, HER2-negative disease. The standard dose is 500 mg by intramuscular injection given as two 250 mg/5 mL injections (one in each buttock) on Days 1, 15, and 29, then once monthly. It binds and degrades the estrogen receptor, blocking estrogen-driven tumor growth. Key risks include embryo-fetal toxicity, injection-site reactions (including sciatic nerve-related events), bleeding with IM injection in patients with bleeding disorders or on anticoagulants, and elevated hepatic enzymes; the dose is reduced to 250 mg in moderate hepatic impairment.
indications: Monotherapy for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women not previously treated with endocrine therapy
Monotherapy for HR-positive advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women with disease progression following endocrine therapy

In combination with ribociclib for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in postmenopausal women, as initial endocrine-based therapy or after progression on endocrine therapy
In combination with palbociclib or abemaciclib for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in women with disease progression after endocrine therapy

moa: Many breast cancers express estrogen receptors (ER) and are stimulated to grow by estrogen. Fulvestrant is an estrogen receptor antagonist that binds the ER competitively with an affinity comparable to estradiol, and unlike tamoxifen it has no agonist activity. Binding leads to downregulation and degradation of the ER protein in breast cancer cells (a selective estrogen receptor degrader, SERD), thereby blocking estrogen-driven tumor growth. It inhibits the growth of both estrogen-sensitive and tamoxifen-resistant human breast cancer cell lines and xenografts. In postmenopausal women, fulvestrant does not change plasma FSH or LH, indicating no peripheral steroidal effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to fulvestrant or any component (reactions include urticaria and angioedema)
relative: Bleeding diatheses, thrombocytopenia, or anticoagulant use (IM injection bleeding risk)
Moderate hepatic impairment (use reduced 250 mg dose)
Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C; not studied)
Pregnancy / females of reproductive potential not using contraception

preg: Can cause fetal harm based on animal data and its mechanism of action. In pregnant rats and rabbits, fulvestrant given during organogenesis caused embryo-fetal toxicity, including skeletal malformations and fetal loss, at doses far below the maximum recommended human dose. There are no data in pregnant women. Verify pregnancy status before starting and advise pregnant women of the potential risk to a fetus. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 1 year after the last dose.
lact: There is no information on the presence of fulvestrant in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production; it is detected in rat milk at levels about 12-fold higher than plasma. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed infant, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 1 year after the final dose.
renal: Renal elimination is negligible (less than 1%), so no dose adjustment is needed and a dedicated renal impairment study was not conducted. Fulvestrant concentrations in women with creatinine clearance as low as 30 mL/min were similar to those with normal renal function; it has not been studied below 30 mL/min.
hepatic: Fulvestrant is metabolized primarily in the liver. Mild impairment (Child-Pugh A) gives exposure comparable to normal function, so no change is needed. In moderate impairment (Child-Pugh B), AUC increased by about 70%, so a reduced dose of 250 mg is recommended. It has not been studied in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C).

minor: CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers - no clinically relevant effect; ketoconazole and rifampin did not alter fulvestrant pharmacokinetics, no dose adjustment needed
interactions.food: Not applicable - administered by intramuscular injection.
interactions.alcohol: No specific drug-alcohol interaction is described; note the injection vehicle contains alcohol and benzyl alcohol excipients.
interactions.diagnostics: Due to structural similarity to estradiol, fulvestrant interferes with immunoassay measurement of serum estradiol, producing falsely elevated estradiol levels - use an alternative (e.g., mass spectrometry-based) method if estradiol must be measured.

common: Back pain, pain in extremity, musculoskeletal pain
Elevated hepatic enzymes (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase)
serious: Hypersensitivity reactions including urticaria and angioedema
Injection-site reactions with sciatica, neuralgia, neuropathic pain, or peripheral neuropathy
Bleeding/hematoma at injection site in patients with bleeding disorders or on anticoagulants
Thromboembolic events (notably in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors)
Myelosuppression (neutropenia, leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia) when combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors
rare: Vaginal bleeding (mainly in the first 6 weeks after switching from prior hormonal therapy)
emergency: Signs of venous thromboembolism (leg swelling, chest pain, breathlessness)
Febrile neutropenia or sepsis (with combination therapy)

monitoring: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin)
Coagulation status / platelet count in patients at bleeding risk
Complete blood count when combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor
Pregnancy status before initiation in females of reproductive potential
counsel: This medicine is given as two injections into the buttocks at the clinic on Days 1, 15, and 29, then once a month
Injection-site pain or numbness, and aches in joints, bones, or muscles are common - report severe or persistent pain or new leg/buttock numbness
Tell your provider if you have a bleeding disorder or take blood thinners (e.g., warfarin)
It can harm an unborn baby - use effective contraception during treatment and for 1 year after the last dose, and report a known or suspected pregnancy
Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 1 year after the final dose
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or signs of an allergic reaction (swelling, rash, trouble breathing)
pk: Dose-related ER downregulation seen within ~15-22 days; additional Day 15 dose helps reach steady state in the first month
Cmax ~25-28 ng/mL after 500 mg IM (single dose Cmax ~25.1 ng/mL)
Apparent half-life about 40 days (depot IM release)
Once-monthly dosing maintains steady-state exposure (Cmin ~12-16 ng/mL)
Refrigerate 2-8 C (36-46 F); protect from light, keep in original carton until use
pearls: Pure ER antagonist and SERD with no agonist activity - effective in tamoxifen-resistant disease
Standard 500 mg dose is two 250 mg/5 mL IM injections, one in each buttock, on Days 1, 15, 29, then monthly; the Day 15 loading dose speeds steady state
Reduce to 250 mg in moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B); not studied in severe
Use caution with IM injection in patients with bleeding disorders, thrombocytopenia, or on anticoagulants
Falsely elevates estradiol on immunoassays - use a non-immunoassay method if measurement is needed
Pre/perimenopausal women receiving combination CDK4/6 therapy require an LHRH agonist
No clinically significant drug-drug interactions, including with CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers
missed: Fulvestrant is administered by a healthcare provider on a fixed schedule (Days 1, 15, 29, then monthly). If a scheduled injection is missed, contact the clinic to reschedule as soon as possible and resume the monthly schedule per the provider's instructions; do not double the dose.
overdose: Human experience with overdose is limited. No adverse reactions occurred in healthy volunteers given intravenous fulvestrant producing peak concentrations 10-15 times those after IM injection, though toxicity at such levels in cancer patients is unknown. There is no specific antidote; manage with general supportive care and treat symptomatically.
